1.title: LLM and Technical Fundamentals
1.text: Welcome to Module seven: L L M and Technical Fundamentals. This module covers the skills l l m fundamentals, technical fundamentals. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. L L M (large language model) basics: tokens, context windows, sampling, non-determinism, next-token generation. Model options: fast mode, adaptive and extended thinking, effort levels. Fundamental prompting techniques: zero-shot, single-shot, multi-shot. Technical fundamentals: S D K s (software development kit) that wrap R E S T A P I s (application programming interface), streaming and websockets.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater Meets Strange Behavior
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater Meets Strange Behavior. The assistant gave two slightly different answers to the same question. A long claim file made it cut off a list in the middle of a sentence. A developer asks: "Is it broken?".

1.title: How an LLM Works (the Parts the Exam Needs)
1.text: How an L L M Works (the Parts the Exam Needs). The figure shows this: How generation works: text becomes tokens, the model predicts the next token from the context, one token is sampled, and the loop repeats until the end or max tokens.

1.title: How an LLM Works (the Parts the Exam Needs), continued
1.text: How an L L M Works (the Parts the Exam Needs), continued. Token. A piece of text (a word, part of a word or punctuation). Models read, produce and bill in tokens; a token is not a word (a rough rule is about three quarters of a word of English per token). Context window. The maximum tokens the model can consider in one request, input plus output; current models offer up to one million tokens. max tokens. A cap on the output only; if reached, the reply is cut off (stop reason: max tokens).

1.title: How an LLM Works (the Parts the Exam Needs), continued
1.text: How an L L M Works (the Parts the Exam Needs), continued. Next-token generation. The model predicts a probability for every possible next token, one is chosen, appended, and the process repeats. Sampling. How the next token is chosen from the probabilities (temperature, top-p, top-k control randomness). Non-determinism. The same prompt can give different wording each time; do not expect byte-identical output. Hallucination. Fluent text that is not grounded in the input or facts; reduce with grounding, citations and validation.

1.title: How an LLM Works (the Parts the Exam Needs), continued
1.text: How an L L M Works (the Parts the Exam Needs), continued. Why answers differ: sampling is random by design, and small changes in the prompt or context shift the probabilities. For repeatable behavior, constrain the output (structured output, clear instructions, evals) rather than hope for identical text. Why output was cut off: a long reply reached max tokens; raise the cap or ask for a shorter answer (not a bug).

1.title: How an LLM Works (the Parts the Exam Needs), continued
1.text: How an L L M Works (the Parts the Exam Needs), continued. On current models the sampling parameters temperature, top p and top k are not supported: a non-default value returns a four hundred error. Guide behavior with prompting and effort instead. On older models they could be set (low temperature for more consistent, high for more varied output). As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: Questions about "making output more random or more consistent" test the concept (sampling and non-determinism); on current models the practical levers are prompt design, structured output and effort.

1.title: Model Options: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode
1.text: Model Options: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode. Adaptive thinking. What it changes: The model decides how much to reason before answering. Trade-off: Better on hard problems; thinking tokens cost output price and time. Extended thinking. What it changes: A manual reasoning budget on older models. Trade-off: Rejected on current models. Effort. What it changes: low to max: overall thoroughness and token use. Trade-off: Higher equals better quality and slower, costlier. Fast mode. What it changes: Faster output at a premium price on supported models. Trade-off: Pay more for speed. (The request parameters are in Module three; here you need to know what each is for.).

1.title: Model Options: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode, continued
1.text: Model Options: Thinking, Effort and Fast Mode, continued. The figure shows this: Every option moves quality, latency and cost: higher effort and thinking buy quality, fast mode buys speed, smaller models buy price and speed. Exam tip: Effort and thinking trade quality for cost and latency; fast mode trades price for speed.

1.title: Fundamental Prompting Techniques
1.text: Fundamental Prompting Techniques. Zero-shot. What it is: Instructions only, no examples. Use it when: The task is simple and well described. Single-shot (one-shot). What it is: One example of input and output. Use it when: You need to show the format or style. Multi-shot (few-shot). What it is: Several examples, including tricky cases. Use it when: Consistency matters or the task is ambiguous; examples teach the pattern better than long rules. Examples should be diverse and representative, include edge cases, and match the exact output format you want.

1.title: Technical Fundamentals
1.text: Technical Fundamentals. S D K s wrap R E S T A P I s. The official Python and Type Script S D K s build the H T T P request, add headers, parse Jason (Java Script Object Notation), retry transient errors, and offer streaming helpers. You can call the R E S T endpoint directly, but the S D K saves effort and handles retries. Authentication is an A P I key sent with the request (the S D K reads A N T H R O P I C A P I K E Y); cloud platforms use their own identity (Module three). Streaming uses server-sent events (S S E) over H T T P: one-way, server to client, simple through proxies. Websockets are a two-way, persistent connection used by some real-time products; know the difference: S S E is one-way text streaming, websockets are full-duplex.

1.title: Technical Fundamentals, continued
1.text: Technical Fundamentals, continued. Timeouts and retries: set client timeouts that fit long generations; use exponential backoff; make retries safe (Module one). Context management is an application job (Module nine): the A P I does not trim your history for you.

2.title: Technical Fundamentals, continued
2.text: Technical Fundamentals, continued. The figure shows this: R E S T returns a full response; S S E streams events one way; websockets keep a two-way connection open. Exam tip: S S E streams one way over H T T P (the Messages A P I streaming); websockets keep a two-way connection.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Token: Piece of text; basis of limits and billing. Context window: Max tokens in one request (input plus output); up to one million on current models. max tokens: Output cap; hitting it truncates. Generation: Next-token prediction, one token at a time, sampled. Non-determinism: Same prompt can vary; constrain with structure and evals. Sampling params: temperature, top p, top k: concept; not supported on current models (four hundred error). Model options: Adaptive thinking, effort (low, max), fast mode (speed at a premium). Shots: Zero-shot (instructions), single-shot (one example), multi-shot (several, with edge cases). Transport: S D K s wrap R E S T; S S E equals one-way stream; websockets equals two-way connection.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A developer sends the same prompt twice and gets two slightly different answers. What does this show? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Next-token sampling makes outputs non-deterministic; use constraints and evals for consistency.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A reply stops mid-sentence and stop reason is max tokens. What is the right interpretation? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. max tokens limits output; reaching it truncates the answer.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. What is a token? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Tokens are the units of text for context limits and pricing.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. What does the context window limit? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The window covers input plus output for the request.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A developer wants to show the model the exact output layout with one worked example. Which technique is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. One input and output example is single-shot prompting.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which task most benefits from multi-shot prompting? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Several diverse examples teach the pattern and edge-case handling.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. What is the practical difference between S S E and websockets? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The Messages A P I streams over S S E; websockets are full-duplex.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. Why use an official S D K instead of raw H T T P calls? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. S D K s reduce boilerplate and add retry and streaming support.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. A developer tries to set temperature on a current model and gets a four hundred error. What should they do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Current models do not accept non-default sampling parameters.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Select two. Which two statements about generation are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are C and D. Generation is next-token prediction, and grounding and validation reduce hallucination; outputs vary and tokens are not words.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. Select two. Which two describe fast mode and effort correctly? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Fast mode buys speed at a premium and effort is a behavioral signal that trades quality for cost and latency.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all eleven answers. Question one: C. Question two: B. Question three: A. Question four: B. Question five: D. Question six: B. Question seven: B. Question eight: B. Question nine: A. Question ten: C and D. Question eleven: B and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
